To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mutations in the V. cholerae OmpU porins affect pore properties in different ways, and the results are consistent with a homology model of the protein.
mutations in the L3 loop and barrel wall residues of OmpU affect pore permeability to nutrients, antibiotics, and external signaling compounds.
the phenotypes of V. cholerae OmpU mutants can be interpreted in terms of homology models and that the phenotypes observed are not identical to those of the E. coli porin mutants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the functional characterization of the pore region of the OmpU channel and the identification of residues involved in the permeation of specific compounds.
the functional characterization of the OmpU pore, which is the major outer membrane channel of V. cholerae, a major intestinal pathogen.

the identification of residues involved in the control of pore permeability, a key property for the physiology of V. cholerae and other pathogens that use porins for the uptake of nutrients and external signals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
OmpU is a very versatile porin with a large number of residues involved in the control of its function.

OmpU, a member of a family of porins that are widely conserved in the Proteobacteria, is a versatile channel that controls the permeability of V. cholerae to a wide range of compounds, including large sugars and sodium deoxycholates, and is a major factor controlling the response of this intestinal pathogenic bacterium to bile salts.
the V. cholerae porin OmpU is a highly versatile protein that can be modulated in a variety of ways to allow the passage of specific nutrients, antibiotics, and signaling compounds.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pore properties of the porins of V. cholerae are determined by the same residues as in the E. coli porin OmpF, but with some differences in the relative contribution of the residues.
OmpU is more similar to OmpF than to OmpC, as far as pore properties and antibiotic sensitivity are concerned, although OmpC and OmpU share the same function in the V. cholerae outer membrane.

the V. cholerae porin OmpU, like other porins, is a multifaceted protein that controls the permeability of its host to various compounds, including nutrients and signals, in a manner that depends on the nature of the compound.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the V. cholerae porin OmpU can be used as a model for the analysis of the role of specific residues in the control of the passage of compounds across the outer membrane.
the pore properties and functions of the V. cholerae porin OmpU are not identical to those of its E. coli homologs, OmpC and OmpF.
, despite the high degree of sequence and structure conservation between porins, the specific residues that control pore properties are not conserved.
